error_modes.label: Knowledge of the exercises given as daily assignment for the navigation sortie

texts.0: SP, due to lack of knowledge of the published procedure for the condition encountered, could not state the legs, the turning points or the completion criteria of the exercises given as daily assignment for the navigation sortie. SP did not know in detail all exercises given as daily assignment, so the IP had to present the whole route and the associated exercises from the beginning at the pre-flight briefing. Two assigned exercises had to be demonstrated in flight before SP could attempt them and the planned navigation legs were not completed as briefed.
texts.1: SP, due to a superficial review of the daily assignment, recalled the navigation exercises only in outline and produced the planned headings, times and altitudes only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP. Knowledge of the assigned exercises stayed at the minimum acceptable limit and the sequence of legs had to be restated verbally before each turning point. SP flew the complete route, but the delay in recall left no time for the last assigned exercise.
texts.2: SP, due to studying the daily assignment late in the preparation, hesitated on the entry parameters of two exercises of the navigation profile at the pre-flight briefing. SP identified the gap without IP input, returned to the assignment sheet and restated the correct sequence of legs and the completion criteria before the walk-around. The route was then flown as planned and no exercise had to be re-briefed in flight.
texts.3: SP knew in detail all exercises given as daily assignment and stated the sequence of legs, the planned parameters and the completion criteria of each one without hesitation. Answers at the pre-flight briefing were prompt and accurate and the same knowledge was applied over the route without prompting. The post-flight briefing confirmed correct understanding of every assigned exercise.
texts.4: SP knew every exercise of the daily navigation assignment in exceptional detail, including the reason behind each planned parameter and the errors most commonly associated with it. SP briefed the complete route and the associated exercises to the IP without notes and correctly linked each one to the preceding navigation sorties of the syllabus. Every question at the post-flight briefing was answered accurately and with the correct reference.
texts.marginal: SP knew all exercises given as daily assignment to the required standard, but answers on the later legs of the route were slower and less detailed than on the first ones. The trend indicates that preparation is concentrated on the initial part of the assignment. SP is expected to study the whole assignment with the same depth so that recall is uniform over the complete navigation profile.

error_modes.label: Flight Manual, A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and aeronautical publications (MAIP, maps)

texts.0: SP, due to not having reviewed the Flight Manual and the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual before the navigation sortie, quoted an operating limit incorrectly and could not locate the applicable paragraph when asked. SP did not know in detail the publications required for the flight, including AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications (MAIP, maps), and could not find the route data on the chart. The IP had to state the correct limits, read the procedure aloud and identify the chart entries before the sortie could be briefed.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete study of the Flight Manual and the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, produced the correct limit only after the IP indicated the chapter to be opened, and located the MAIP entry for the en-route airfield only after being told where to look. Knowledge of the required publications remained at the minimum acceptable limit and every reference had to be confirmed verbally by the IP. SP finally quoted the correct paragraph and chart data, but the search delayed the pre-flight briefing.
texts.2: SP, due to relying on memory instead of the current publication, misstated one value of the Flight Manual limits at the pre-flight briefing of the navigation sortie. SP recognized the error without IP intervention, opened the manual and gave the correct value together with its paragraph within a few seconds. The remaining questions on the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications (MAIP, maps) were answered accurately.
texts.3: SP knew in detail the Flight Manual, the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications (MAIP, maps) and used them with confidence throughout the navigation sortie. Limits, normal procedures, the applicable VFR rules and the route and airfield data were quoted correctly and with the right reference at both briefings. No answer required correction by the IP.
texts.4: SP used all handbooks related to the flight with complete confidence, quoting limits and procedures verbatim together with chapter and paragraph, and reading the route directly from the current chart and MAIP entries. SP also explained how the Flight Manual limits and the AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 rules applied to the specific route and conditions of the sortie and cross-checked the information between the publications. Knowledge exceeded the level expected at this stage of the syllabus.
texts.marginal: SP knew the Flight Manual and the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual to the required standard, but answers drawn from AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications (MAIP, maps) were noticeably slower and more general. The trend shows that study is concentrated on the aircraft handbooks and not on the regulatory and navigation publications, which carry most of the information used on this category. SP is expected to study all handbooks required by BD 3-1/HATC with the same depth so that every reference is used with equal confidence.

error_modes.label: Knowledge of meteorological principles and attendance of the morning meteorological briefing

texts.0: SP, due to mission planning that did not address the forecast weather at the recovery time, could not interpret the wind, visibility and cloud information given at the morning meteorological briefing for the route. SP did not have knowledge of meteorological principles and could not follow the briefing without problem, and the IP had to explain the significance of the forecast for each leg. The visibility trend along the route was not identified at all and the sortie profile had to be reconstructed by the IP.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete preparation on meteorology, followed the morning meteorological briefing only in general terms and stated the effect of the forecast on the route only after the IP asked directed questions. Knowledge of meteorological principles stayed at the minimum acceptable limit and the implications for the en-route legs had to be drawn out verbally. SP finally identified the deteriorating visibility on the return leg, but only after being prompted twice.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried reading of the forecast before the morning meteorological briefing, initially misjudged the significance of the wind change forecast for the middle leg of the route. SP re-examined the charts without IP intervention, corrected the assessment and stated the expected drift and the visibility trend before the crew briefing ended. The remaining meteorological information was interpreted correctly and used in the route plan.
texts.3: SP has knowledge of meteorological principles and attended the morning meteorological briefing without problem, interpreting the forecast wind, cloud and visibility for every leg of the route. SP stated the expected drift, the effect on leg times and the conditions expected at the recovery time accurately and without prompting. All meteorological questions at the post-flight briefing were answered correctly.
texts.4: SP interpreted the morning meteorological briefing with exceptional depth, explaining the mechanism behind the forecast conditions and the expected changes over the duration of the navigation sortie. SP linked the forecast to the specific legs of the route, stated the points where visibility could fall below VFR requirements and proposed the associated decision points before being asked. The assessment made during the briefing was confirmed by the actual conditions encountered.
texts.marginal: SP has the required knowledge of meteorological principles and followed the morning meteorological briefing without problem, but the interpretation stayed close to the printed forecast values without extending to their effect on the individual legs. The trend indicates that meteorological information is received correctly but is not yet fully converted into route planning. SP is expected to reach the point where every forecast element is translated directly into the expected conditions and timings of the navigation profile.

error_modes.label: Aerodynamics knowledge and theoretical explanation of situations encountered in flight

texts.0: SP, due to not having studied the aerodynamics material supporting the navigation phase, could not explain theoretically the change in performance observed during the climb and the cruise legs of the sortie. SP does not have aerodynamics knowledge sufficient to explain situations to be encountered during flight, and gave contradictory answers on the relation between power, airspeed and fuel flow at cruise altitude. The IP had to teach the theoretical background at the post-flight briefing before the sortie could be debriefed.
texts.1: SP, due to superficial study of the theory, explained the aerodynamic behaviour observed on the route only in general terms and reached the correct explanation only after successive verbal indications from the IP. Aerodynamics knowledge remained at the minimum acceptable limit and the answers on cruise performance and on the effect of the turn on the ground track needed continuous guidance. The explanation was eventually complete, but it was produced by the IP's questions rather than by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to confusing two related concepts, first gave an incorrect theoretical explanation of the airspeed change observed during the climbing leg. SP recognized the inconsistency without IP intervention, reconsidered the reasoning and gave the correct explanation of the relation between power, weight and airspeed within the same answer. The remaining theoretical questions on the situations encountered during the navigation sortie were answered correctly.
texts.3: SP has aerodynamics knowledge and explained theoretically every situation encountered during the navigation sortie, including cruise performance, the effect of the turns on the ground track and the behaviour of the aircraft at the planned altitudes. The explanations were accurate, given without hesitation and correctly connected to what was actually observed in flight. No theoretical answer needed correction by the IP.
texts.4: SP explained the aerodynamics of the navigation profile at a level beyond that expected at this stage, connecting cruise performance, altitude selection and fuel flow into a single consistent picture. SP predicted before the flight how the aircraft would behave on each leg at the planned weight and altitude and confirmed the prediction against the actual figures at the post-flight briefing. Every theoretical question was answered with the correct reasoning and the correct reference.
texts.marginal: SP has the required aerodynamics knowledge and explained the situations encountered during flight to the acceptable standard, but the answers stayed at the level of definitions and did not always extend to the specific conditions of the sortie. The trend indicates that theory is retained but is not yet applied readily to what is observed on the route. SP is expected to link every theoretical concept directly to the performance seen during the navigation legs.

error_modes.label: Knowledge of airport traffic procedures and ability to plan a flight

texts.0: SP, due to lack of awareness of a published restriction that was available in the briefing material, could not state the traffic procedures of the en-route and alternate airfields used in the navigation plan. SP does not know airport traffic procedures and does not have sufficient knowledge in order to plan a flight, and the route, the fuel figures and the alternate selection had to be produced by the IP. The flight plan presented at the pre-flight briefing was not usable and was rewritten before departure.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete study of the airfield data, presented a flight plan in which the entry procedure for the en-route airfield and the fuel reserve were corrected only after successive verbal indications from the IP. Knowledge of airport traffic procedures remained at the minimum acceptable limit and each element of the plan had to be checked verbally before it was accepted. The plan was finally correct, but the corrections delayed the briefing and were not initiated by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to using an outdated note instead of the current publication, initially planned the arrival at the en-route airfield with the wrong pattern direction. SP identified the discrepancy without IP intervention, checked the current MAIP entry and corrected the arrival procedure and the associated timing before the plan was presented. The rest of the flight plan, including the alternate and the fuel figures, was complete and correct.
texts.3: SP knows airport traffic procedures and has sufficient knowledge in order to plan a flight, and presented a complete navigation plan with correct route, timings, fuel figures, alternate and airfield entry and exit procedures. All questions on the traffic procedures of the departure, en-route and alternate airfields were answered accurately and without prompting. The plan was accepted at the pre-flight briefing without correction.
texts.4: SP planned the navigation sortie to a standard above that expected at this stage, presenting the route with alternative options for the alternate airfield and the associated fuel and timing consequences of each one. SP quoted the traffic procedures of every airfield on the route together with the applicable restrictions and their source, and identified in advance the points where a change of plan would be required. The plan needed no correction and was used as briefed.
texts.marginal: SP knows airport traffic procedures and planned the flight to the required standard, but the planning of the alternate and of the en-route diversion options was noticeably less developed than the planning of the primary route. The trend indicates that preparation is concentrated on the intended profile rather than on its alternatives. SP is expected to plan the alternate and diversion options with the same completeness as the primary route.

error_modes.label: Knowledge of air medicine and flight physiology, and interpretation of physiological conditions and flight effects

texts.0: SP, due to not having studied the air medicine material of the phase, could not interpret the physiological conditions and flight effects associated with the altitudes and the duration of the navigation sortie. SP does not have knowledge of air medicine and flight physiology and gave incorrect answers on the recognition and the immediate actions for hypoxia and for the visual illusions expected over featureless terrain. The IP had to teach the recognition criteria and the corrective actions before the sortie could be debriefed.
texts.1: SP, due to superficial study of flight physiology, described the physiological effects expected on the route only in general terms and gave the recognition signs and the required actions only after directed questions from the IP. Knowledge of air medicine remained at the minimum acceptable limit and the connection between the planned altitudes, the sortie duration and the expected effects had to be drawn out verbally. The answers were finally correct, but they were reached with continuous guidance.
texts.2: SP, due to confusing the symptoms of two related conditions, first gave an incomplete description of the effects expected during the higher legs of the navigation profile. SP corrected the answer without IP intervention, separated the two conditions and stated the recognition signs and the required actions for each one accurately. The remaining questions on flight physiology and on the effects of the sortie duration were answered correctly.
texts.3: SP has knowledge of air medicine and flight physiology and interpreted correctly all the physiological conditions and flight effects to be encountered on the navigation sortie. SP stated the recognition signs, the immediate actions and the preventive measures for the altitudes, the duration and the visual environment of the route without prompting. All questions at the post-flight briefing were answered accurately.
texts.4: SP interpreted the physiological aspects of the navigation profile at a level beyond that expected at this stage, connecting altitude, sortie duration, hydration and visual environment into a single assessment of personal fitness for the flight. SP described the recognition signs and the required actions for each expected effect and stated in advance the points of the route where the risk would be highest. Every answer was accurate and supported by the correct reference.
texts.marginal: SP has the required knowledge of air medicine and flight physiology and interpreted the expected conditions to the acceptable standard, but the answers on the visual illusions associated with long legs over uniform terrain were less complete than the rest. The trend indicates that the physiological material is known in general but not yet applied fully to the specific environment of navigation flying. SP is expected to cover the visual and fatigue related effects of this category with the same depth as the remaining physiology material.

error_modes.label: Awareness of sea and land survival procedures and of rescue procedures from SAR means

texts.0: SP, due to not having reviewed the survival material before the navigation sortie, could not state the sea and land survival procedures applicable to the terrain and the sea sectors crossed by the planned route. SP is not aware of the rescue procedures from SAR means and could not describe the use of the survival equipment carried or the actions expected after an ejection over the route. The IP had to present the survival and SAR procedures in full before the sortie could be briefed.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete study of the survival procedures, described the actions after a forced landing or ejection along the route only in outline and completed them only after successive verbal indications from the IP. Awareness of the sea and land survival procedures and of the rescue procedures from SAR means remained at the minimum acceptable limit and each step had to be prompted. The description was finally complete, but it was produced by the IP's questions rather than by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to recalling the sequence from memory instead of the publication, initially omitted one step of the sea survival procedure applicable to the coastal leg of the route. SP identified the omission without IP intervention, restated the complete sequence and added the associated actions for contact with SAR means. The land survival procedures and the use of the survival equipment were described correctly and in full.
texts.3: SP is aware of both sea and land survival procedures and of the rescue procedures from SAR means, and described them accurately for the terrain and the sea sectors of the planned route. SP stated the use of the survival equipment, the signalling means and the expected sequence of contact with SAR without prompting. All questions at the pre-flight and post-flight briefings were answered correctly.
texts.4: SP described the sea and land survival procedures and the rescue procedures from SAR means in exceptional detail and applied them specifically to each sector of the navigation route. SP identified the terrain and sea areas along the route where each procedure would apply, stated the signalling and communication means available in each case and explained the sequence of actions from the moment of the emergency to the recovery. Every answer was accurate and supported by the correct reference.
texts.marginal: SP is aware of both sea and land survival procedures and of the rescue procedures from SAR means to the required standard, but the description of the sea sector procedures was less detailed and slower than that of the land procedures. The trend indicates that preparation is concentrated on the part of the route flown over land. SP is expected to know the sea survival and SAR procedures with the same completeness, since the planned routes of this category include sectors over water.
